title: Can Cobre Panama copper mine run for 25 years without growing?
gist: A Panamanian government commission recommended Cobre Panama reopen for 25 years without expanding its physical footprint, but Benchmark's Piotr Kulas argues this is impossible: the only existing pit, Botija, holds ~551Mt (about a fifth of contained copper, 5-6 years at the 100 Mtpa mill rate), while the 2,700Mt reserve requires seven pits. Political cycles and First Quantum's >$27bn compensation claim tied to the 'zero cost to taxpayer' condition further cloud a restart.

insights.claim: Panama's government commission recommended Cobre Panama operate for 25 years without expanding its physical footprint, steadily shrinking it, followed by eight years of active closure and 30 years of post-closure monitoring.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: The headline '25-year life' comes with a framework that structurally caps output growth.
insights.quote: has recommended 25 years of operation but without expanding the site’s physical footprint
insights.locator: A commission convened by Panama’s government

insights.claim: Non-negotiable reopening criteria include compliance with Supreme Court rulings, state ownership, financial self-sufficiency, data transparency, international-standard supervision and priority for affected communities.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: State ownership as a precondition changes First Quantum's equity economics materially.
insights.quote: Other non-negotiable criteria for reopening the site include compliance with existing Supreme Court rulings and laws around the project, ownership by the state, and the project must be financially self-sustaining.
insights.locator: The report also recommends steadily shrinking

insights.claim: Benchmark's lead copper analyst says it is not possible to run Cobre Panama for 25 years without physical expansion because the reserve plan relies on seven pits while only one exists.
insights.speaker: Piotr Kulas
insights.so_what: Either the 25-year life is fiction or the 'no expansion' condition will be quietly relaxed; both matter for copper supply models.
insights.quote: It will not be possible to operate the project for 25 years without physical expansion.
insights.locator: Currently operating pit only sufficient for five to six years

insights.claim: Cobre Panama's reserve is 2,700Mt of ore at 0.38% copper, but the mining zone needed to deliver it is much larger than today's disturbed area.
insights.speaker: Piotr Kulas
insights.so_what: Analysts treating reserve as one number overstate deliverable supply under a footprint cap.
insights.quote: While most analysts treat the reserve as a single number, 2,700Mt of ore at a modest 0.38% copper
insights.locator: Currently operating pit only sufficient for five to six years

insights.claim: The Botija pit holds 551Mt of reserve, about a fifth of contained copper, equal to roughly five to six years at full plant capacity of 100 Mtpa.
insights.speaker: Piotr Kulas
insights.so_what: Without new pits, throughput must fall within a few years of restart, cutting copper output well below the 2022 level.
insights.quote: Botija holds 551Mt of reserve, about a fifth of the project's contained copper. That is roughly five to six years at full plant capacity.

insights.claim: Cobre Panama produced 350kt of contained copper in 2022, but under a no-expansion regime that figure could become much smaller.
insights.speaker: Piotr Kulas
insights.so_what: Copper balance models assuming a return to ~350kt/yr from Cobre Panama are likely too optimistic.
insights.quote: The site produced 350kt copper contained in 2022, but this number could become much smaller.

insights.claim: The planned Colina and Medio pits together hold 37% of contained copper, more than Botija, and satellite imagery shows the access road to Colina is already complete.
insights.speaker: Piotr Kulas
insights.so_what: Infrastructure for expansion is already in place, so the binding constraint is political permission, not engineering.
insights.quote: Satellite imagery shows the access road to the Colina pit area, the next due for development, is complete.
insights.locator: The planned Colina and Medio pits

insights.claim: Developing Colina requires clearing thousands of hectares of jungle and a river diversion, which would increase the mine's footprint and is likely to be politically contentious.
insights.speaker: Piotr Kulas
insights.so_what: Expansion runs directly into the environmental concerns that triggered the 2023 closure.
insights.quote: Mining Colina requires the clearance of thousands of hectares of jungle and a river diversion, increasing the mine’s footprint.
insights.locator: The planned Colina and Medio pits

themes.theme: Political and legal risk to restart

insights.claim: A state-commissioned SGS audit found 98.9% compliance across 370 environmental commitments under the previous operation, suggesting some commission demands were already met.
insights.speaker: Piotr Kulas
insights.so_what: The prior environmental record undercuts claims the mine was non-compliant, supporting a restart case.
insights.quote: The state commissioned SGS audit found 98.9% compliance across the 370 environmental commitments.
insights.locator: “The report is only a recommendation,” Kulas noted.

insights.claim: Panama's single five-year presidential terms mean a 25-year mine plan spans five administrations, with mixed public opinion making protests on any restart likely.
insights.speaker: Piotr Kulas
insights.so_what: Political-cycle risk caps the valuation multiple any investor should pay for Cobre Panama's long-life output.
insights.quote: A 25-year plan spans five administrations, and public opinion on the mine is mixed. Any restart will come with issues and protests.
insights.locator: He added: “Politics in Panama are complicated.

insights.claim: Kulas suggests the commission may be framing a normal mining operation in novel language, while asserting the mine will not run 25 years without significantly growing its footprint.
insights.speaker: Piotr Kulas
insights.so_what: Expect the 'no expansion' wording to be reinterpreted rather than enforced if the mine restarts.
insights.quote: Perhaps the report is framing a normal operation in novel language.
insights.locator: He added: “Politics in Panama are complicated.

themes.theme: Zero-taxpayer-cost condition and First Quantum's claim

insights.claim: The requirement that the mine operate at zero cost to the taxpayer is the most consequential condition, because it covers closure and rehabilitation of a very large site.
insights.speaker: Piotr Kulas
insights.so_what: Closure liabilities must be funded by operations, raising the required operating life and cash generation.
insights.quote: This requirement covers closure and rehabilitation of a very large site,
insights.locator: Cost requirement could be a challenge

insights.claim: The commission makes the end of First Quantum's court case against Panama a mandatory condition for reopening, while First Quantum claims minimum compensation exceeding US$27 billion.
insights.speaker: Piotr Kulas
insights.so_what: Restart is a negotiated settlement: First Quantum trades its >$27bn claim for operating cash flows.
insights.quote: The company is claiming a minimum compensation exceeding USD $27 billion.
insights.locator: Cost requirement could be a challenge

insights.claim: First Quantum and partners would drop their claims only if the 'open to close' phase generates enough revenue to repay the capex incurred to build the mine, which creates pressure for a larger, longer operation.
insights.speaker: Piotr Kulas
insights.so_what: Capex payback economics are incompatible with a shrinking-footprint plan, so the expansion question is central to any settlement.
insights.quote: First Quantum and its partners would drop them only if the ‘open to close’ phase generates enough revenue to pay back for the substantial capex they incurred to open the mine in the first place.
insights.locator: Cost requirement could be a challenge
